title: One bright mode is enough: exact finite-copy Gaussian Fisher information for pure single-mode models
shortTitle: The best way to measure many copies of a light beam
oneLine: For m copies of a pure single-mode Gaussian state, no Gaussian measurement beats combining the copies into one bright output and measuring every output by homodyne detection; the exact optimum is a one-angle formula.
abstract: A small change in a light beam can be read off by measuring field quadratures. With only Gaussian measurements, measuring m identical copies jointly can give more Fisher information than measuring them one by one, as Navarro, Morelli, Sanz and Mehboudi showed with an interferometer that concentrates the changing mean into one bright output; they left open which Gaussian measurement is best for a finite number of copies. For every smooth one-parameter family of pure single-mode Gaussian states and every m, this candidate proves that the maximum Fisher information over all fixed Gaussian measurements, including ancilla-assisted schemes, equals (m−1)λ²/2 + max over φ of [2m(a cos φ + b sin φ)² + (λ²/2) cos² 2φ], in normalised coordinates where (a, b) is the rate of change of the mean and λ that of the squeezing. It is attained by the concentration interferometer, homodyne detection of the dark outputs along a fixed axis and one optimised homodyne angle on the bright output. The same argument gives the exact optimum when measurement-seed squeezing is capped, an exact formula for the shortfall from the quantum Fisher information (nondecreasing in m, at most λ²/2 in total, with an explicit limit), and a necessary and sufficient condition for joint measurement to help. The interferometer is due to Navarro et al.; the new part is the finite-copy upper bound and its consequences. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Exact finite-copy optimum (Theorem 1, proof): for a pure single-mode Gaussian family in normal form σ=I, σ′=λ·diag(1,−1), d′=(a,b), the best Fisher information over all fixed Gaussian measurements on m copies, including ancillas, is (m−1)λ²/2 + max_φ[2m(a cos φ + b sin φ)² + (λ²/2)cos²2φ].

Attaining measurement (Theorem 1, proof): a passive interferometer that adds the copies coherently into one bright output, a homodyne at the optimal angle φ on that output and q-homodyne on the m−1 dark outputs; no active squeezing element is needed.

Capped measurement squeezing (Theorem 2, proof): for pure general-dyne seeds with e^(−R) ≤ M ≤ e^R in normalised coordinates, the optimum is again a one-variable concave problem attained by the same interferometer.

Distance from the quantum limit (Corollary 1, proof): with Q = 2(a²+b²) + λ²/2 the one-copy quantum Fisher information, the shortfall mQ − F_m is nondecreasing in m, never exceeds λ²/2, tends to 2λ²a²b²/(a²+b²)², and vanishes exactly when λab = 0.

When joint measurement helps (Proposition 1, proof): for m ≥ 2 the optimum beats m times the single-copy optimum exactly when det[w, Aw] ≠ 0, that is, when the mean moves in a direction that is not an axis of the changing noise ellipse.
Coherent-squeezing example (Section 4.5, exact): the value 2m + 4mα² − 2 of Navarro et al. is optimal whenever mα² ≥ 2; below that the optimum is 2m + 2mα² + (mα²)²/2.

narration: What is the best way to measure many copies of a light beam? An Evidence Press briefing. Many precision experiments read a tiny change in a beam of light by measuring its electric field with a technique called homodyne detection. If you can prepare the same beam several times, you can measure each copy on its own, or combine the copies first. Quantum theory says the information from separate copies simply adds up. But if you restrict yourself to the standard optical toolbox, mirrors, beam splitters, squeezed light and homodyne detectors, combining the copies can do better. A 2025 paper by Navarro, Morelli, Sanz and Mehboudi showed this, using an interferometer that gathers the changing brightness of all the copies into one output beam, while the other outputs keep only the changing noise. They left open whether that is the best possible scheme for a small number of copies. This release settles the question for every pure single-beam Gaussian state. No measurement built from the standard toolbox, even with extra auxiliary light, beats the simple scheme: gather the signal into one bright output, measure that output at one well chosen angle, and measure every other output along a fixed direction. The best achievable information is given by a short formula. The paper also gives the exact answer when the measurement may use only limited squeezing, and shows that the total shortfall from the quantum limit stays below the noise information of a single copy, however many copies are used. Joint measurement helps exactly when the beam's brightness and its noise change in misaligned directions. The results have written proofs and numerical checks. The interferometer itself is due to the earlier paper; the new part is the proof that nothing beats it. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 31 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
